lessons.title: Minerals: Properties and Identification
lessons.description: How physical properties and acid tests identify the data-sheet minerals.
lessons.content_html:
What Is a Mineral?

Every rock you pick up is made of one or more minerals. Minerals are the building blocks of geology. They form naturally, have a fixed chemical composition, and their atoms arrange themselves into a repeating three-dimensional pattern. Geologists identify minerals not by guessing but by testing a small number of measurable physical properties. Learn those properties and you can name most of the minerals on your data sheet with confidence.

Colour and Streak

Colour is the first thing you notice about a mineral, but it is one of the least reliable identification tools. Many minerals come in several colours because tiny amounts of impurities change the appearance. Quartz, for example, can be colourless, white, pink, purple or smoky grey depending on trace elements present during crystallisation.

Streak is far more reliable. When you drag a mineral across an unglazed porcelain streak plate, it leaves a powder. That powder colour is constant for a given mineral regardless of surface colour variations. Haematite is a perfect example: its surface can look silver-grey or red, but its streak is always red-brown. Galena, the lead ore, always gives a grey streak. Calcite always gives a white streak.

Key Fact

Haematite always produces a red-brown streak. Galena gives a grey streak. Calcite gives a white streak. Streak is a more reliable identifier than surface colour because it is unaffected by impurities.

Hardness and the Mohs Scale

Hardness is tested by attempting to scratch one mineral with another, or with a fingernail (hardness about 2.5), a copper coin (about 3.5) or a steel file (about 6.5). A harder mineral will scratch a softer one; a softer one will not mark the harder. The Mohs scale runs from Talc at 1 (scratched by a fingernail) to Diamond at 10 (scratches everything).

The ten reference minerals in order are: Talc (1), Gypsum (2), Calcite (3), Fluorite (4), Apatite (5), Orthoclase feldspar (6), Quartz (7), Topaz (8), Corundum (9), Diamond (10). In exam questions you must use these exact values. A common error is giving quartz as hardness 6 or calcite as hardness 2 — memorise the scale accurately.

Key Fact

The Mohs hardness scale: Talc 1 — Gypsum 2 — Calcite 3 — Fluorite 4 — Apatite 5 — Orthoclase 6 — Quartz 7 — Topaz 8 — Corundum 9 — Diamond 10. Quartz (7) is harder than a steel file (about 6.5) and will scratch glass easily.

Cleavage and Fracture

Cleavage occurs when a mineral breaks along planes of weakness in its crystal lattice. The resulting surfaces are flat and often shiny. Mica breaks into thin flat sheets — it has perfect cleavage in one direction. Feldspar has cleavage in two directions at approximately right angles, producing blocky fragments. Calcite has cleavage in three directions that are not at right angles, producing rhombohedra (diamond-shaped chunks).

Minerals without regular cleavage show fracture instead. Quartz has a conchoidal (shell-like, curved) fracture. Galena has perfect cubic cleavage in three directions at right angles, giving bright flat surfaces that make it look metallic. On the data sheet, pay attention to cleavage descriptions — they distinguish similar-looking minerals.

Lustre

Lustre describes how a mineral surface interacts with light. It is described using standard terms: metallic (galena, haematite), vitreous or glassy (quartz, olivine), pearly (mica), silky (some gypsum varieties), and dull or earthy (some haematite). Metallic lustre always indicates either a native metal or a metallic ore mineral.

The minerals on your data sheet and their most exam-relevant properties:

Quartz — colourless to white, vitreous lustre, hardness 7, conchoidal fracture, no cleavage. Extremely common in granite and sandstone.

Feldspar (orthoclase) — pink or white, vitreous, hardness 6, two cleavage directions at right angles, often showing a blocky shape. Essential mineral in granite.

Mica (biotite / muscovite) — black (biotite) or silvery (muscovite), pearly lustre, hardness about 2.5, perfect single-direction cleavage into thin flexible sheets.

Olivine — olive green, vitreous, hardness 6.5–7, conchoidal fracture, common in basalt and peridotite.

Augite — black to dark green, vitreous to dull, hardness about 5.5–6, two cleavage directions nearly at right angles (compare with hornblende which has cleavage at 60° and 120°).

Calcite — white to colourless, vitreous to pearly, hardness 3, three cleavage directions (rhombohedral), reacts vigorously with dilute hydrochloric acid.

Garnet — red to brown, vitreous, hardness 6.5–7.5, no cleavage (conchoidal fracture), rounded crystal form. Found in metamorphic rocks.

Halite — colourless to white, vitreous, hardness 2.5, cubic cleavage in three directions at right angles, salty taste.

Haematite — silver-grey to red-brown surface, metallic lustre, hardness 5–6, red-brown streak.

Galena — silver-grey, bright metallic lustre, hardness 2.5, perfect cubic cleavage, grey streak, very high density (the main ore of lead).

The Acid Test

Dropping dilute hydrochloric acid onto a mineral surface is a quick and definitive test for calcite. Calcite reacts vigorously, fizzing as carbon dioxide gas is released. This is because calcite is calcium carbonate, and the acid decomposes it. Other carbonate minerals may react slowly or only when powdered. Minerals that are not carbonates, such as quartz, feldspar or mica, do not react at all. In exam questions, if a mineral fizzes with dilute acid, you should identify it as calcite unless the question gives you strong evidence for a different carbonate.

Colour is unreliable for identification. Students often name a mineral solely by colour and are caught out when quartz appears purple (amethyst) or when two minerals share the same colour. Always use at least two properties.

Cleavage surfaces are not the same as crystal faces. Crystal faces form during growth; cleavage surfaces form when you break the mineral. Both may look flat and shiny, but they reflect different internal structures.

Only spec-listed minerals earn marks. Writing “hornfels” or “anorthite” when identifying a hand specimen will score nothing — use only the names listed on your data sheet.

Pulling all these properties together, a systematic approach always works best in your exam. Observe the lustre first (metallic or non-metallic), then test hardness, examine cleavage, check streak colour, and apply the acid test if a carbonate is possible. Each property narrows the field until only one mineral fits. This approach connects directly to the next lesson, where we look at how these minerals originally formed and where they occur in different rock types.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Mineral identification questions on your exam often provide a description of properties and ask you to name the mineral or explain how you would test it. Always state which property you are testing and what result would confirm the identification — for example, “I would scratch it with a steel file (hardness ~6.5): if the mineral is not scratched, its hardness exceeds 6.5, consistent with quartz (7) or garnet (6.5–7.5).” For the acid test, say that vigorous fizzing with dilute HCl confirms calcite because it is a carbonate. Never use colour alone as your sole evidence — examiners will not credit it without supporting properties. Use your data sheet — it lists hardness, streak, lustre and cleavage for every mineral you need.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Minerals are identified using physical properties: colour, streak, hardness (Mohs scale), cleavage, fracture and lustre. Streak is more reliable than surface colour because impurities cannot change it.
  • The Mohs hardness scale runs from Talc (1) to Diamond (10). Key values to know: Calcite = 3, Orthoclase = 6, Quartz = 7.
  • Calcite is uniquely identified by its vigorous fizzing in dilute hydrochloric acid. Only spec-listed mineral names will earn marks in your exam.

lessons.title: How Minerals Form
lessons.description: Crystallisation routes from melt, metamorphism, evaporation, cement and hydrothermal fluids.
lessons.content_html:
Five Routes to a Mineral

Minerals do not simply exist — they form by specific physical or chemical processes. Understanding how a mineral formed tells you a great deal about the environment in which it grew: temperature, pressure, the presence of fluids, and the chemistry available at the time. There are five main formation routes covered by your specification: crystallisation from a melt, metamorphic recrystallisation, evaporation, precipitation from pore waters, and deposition from hydrothermal fluids.

Crystallisation from a Melt

When molten rock — magma — cools, atoms lose energy and begin to join together in a fixed geometric pattern, forming crystals. The size of the resulting crystals depends almost entirely on how quickly the melt cools. Slow cooling deep underground allows atoms to migrate over long distances, producing large, well-formed crystals. Rapid cooling at the surface or in a thin lava flow freezes atoms in place before they can organise into large structures, giving small or even glassy textures.

The minerals that crystallise first from a cooling melt are those that become stable at the highest temperatures. In a typical basaltic magma, olivine and pyroxene (augite) crystallise early. As the melt continues to cool, feldspar and then quartz crystallise later. This sequence — sometimes called Bowen’s reaction series — explains why different igneous rocks contain different mineral assemblages even though they may have started from similar melts.

Key Fact

Crystal size from a melt is controlled by cooling rate: slow cooling (deep igneous bodies) = large crystals; fast cooling (surface lavas or thin intrusions) = small crystals. This is the fundamental link between texture and geological setting in igneous rocks.

Metamorphic Recrystallisation

Recrystallisation occurs when existing minerals in a solid rock are subjected to increased heat and/or pressure. The original mineral grains dissolve or break down in the solid state and atoms reorganise into new, stable minerals suited to the new conditions. Importantly, the rock does not melt — if melting occurs, the process becomes igneous, not metamorphic. Quartz grains in a sandstone, for example, recrystallise under pressure into interlocking crystals of metaquartzite; calcite in a limestone recrystallises into the coarser crystals of marble.

Metamorphic recrystallisation often produces new minerals that were not present in the original rock. Clay minerals in a mudstone transform into mica, chlorite and then garnet as temperature and pressure increase toward the conditions of deep regional metamorphism. These index minerals help geologists map the intensity of metamorphism across a region.

Evaporation

When water evaporates, the dissolved ions it carried become increasingly concentrated until they reach saturation point and begin to precipitate as crystals. Evaporites form in hot, arid environments such as enclosed lagoons, shallow tidal flats or desert lakes. Halite (rock salt) and gypsum are the two most important evaporite minerals. Halite precipitates after most other minerals have already crystallised out; gypsum often precipitates at an earlier stage of evaporation. Thick sequences of evaporite minerals are economically important as a source of salt, fertilisers and building plaster.

Key Fact

Halite and gypsum are evaporite minerals. They crystallise from saline water as it evaporates in hot, arid environments — desert lakes, coastal lagoons and enclosed basins. Their presence in a rock sequence indicates an arid, evaporating palaeoenvironment.

Precipitation from Pore Waters

After sediment grains are deposited, water fills the spaces between them. These pore waters carry dissolved ions. As pressure increases from overlying sediment or as chemistry changes, minerals precipitate out of this water and grow in the pore spaces. This is the process of cementation: calcite, silica or iron oxide cement binds loose grains into solid rock. The type of cement present affects rock strength and permeability enormously — a silica-cemented sandstone is much harder and less permeable than one cemented by calcite.

Hydrothermal fluids are hot, metal-rich waters that circulate along fracture systems in the crust, heated by nearby igneous bodies or by deep burial. As these fluids rise and cool, or encounter a change in pressure or chemistry, metals and other minerals precipitate in the available space, forming veins. The minerals filling a vein are described as a mineral assemblage.

Geologists distinguish between ore minerals (the economically valuable metals, such as galena for lead or haematite for iron) and gangue minerals (the associated but economically valueless minerals, typically quartz or calcite, that fill the vein alongside the ore). Classic hydrothermal vein systems in Britain include lead and zinc veins in the northern Pennines and the tin and copper lodes of Cornwall.

Temperature is a key control on which minerals precipitate from a hydrothermal fluid. High-temperature fluids (above about 300°C) precipitate gold and tungsten minerals; mid-temperature fluids deposit copper and lead sulphides; lower-temperature fluids at depth produce more soluble minerals including carbonates. This zoning pattern is used by mining geologists to target different metals.

A scanning electron microscope (SEM) fires a beam of electrons at a polished mineral surface and detects the signals produced. It can image crystal structure at very high magnification — far beyond what a light microscope allows. The electron microprobe goes further: it uses the same principle to measure the exact chemical composition of a tiny spot on the mineral, letting geologists work out the temperature and pressure conditions under which it formed. Both instruments are used in research laboratories to investigate mineral formation processes that cannot be observed directly in the field.

Linking formation route to environment is a key skill in geology. Seeing large interlocking crystals of quartz and feldspar tells you the rock cooled slowly deep underground. Finding gypsum layers in a sedimentary sequence points to an ancient desert or coastal lagoon. Spotting galena in a quartz vein suggests hydrothermal activity. The next lesson builds on this by looking at how these formation processes produce the distinct textures and mineral compositions we use to classify igneous rocks.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions about mineral formation often ask you to “explain” or “describe the conditions under which” a mineral formed. Make sure your answer links the mineral to the specific environment: for hydrothermal minerals, mention cooling fluids circulating in fractures; for evaporites, mention hot arid conditions and evaporation of seawater or lake water; for magmatic minerals, link crystal size to cooling rate. Avoid vague statements like “it formed by heat” — state which type of heat, at what depth, and what the cooling history was. In extended-response questions, three distinct formation mechanisms with a clear mechanism for each will reach the top band.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Minerals form by five routes: crystallisation from a melt (crystal size controlled by cooling rate), metamorphic recrystallisation (solid-state, no melting), evaporation (producing halite and gypsum), precipitation from pore waters (cement), and deposition from hydrothermal fluids (veins, ore and gangue minerals).
  • Hydrothermal veins contain ore minerals (economically valuable, e.g. galena) alongside gangue minerals (economically valueless, e.g. quartz or calcite).
  • Each formation route leaves a distinctive signature — crystal size, mineral assemblage, setting — that allows geologists to reconstruct the geological history of a rock.

lessons.title: Igneous Rocks: Texture, Mineralogy and Classification
lessons.description: Classify peridotite, basalt, andesite and granite by colour, crystal size and mineralogy.
lessons.content_html:
Igneous Rocks and How They Form

Igneous rocks form when magma cools and solidifies. They can form deep underground, where slow cooling produces coarse-grained rocks, or at the surface where rapid cooling gives fine-grained or glassy textures. Your specification focuses on four igneous rock types: peridotite, basalt, andesite and granite. You must be able to classify these from their colour, crystal size and mineral content — the three properties tested most frequently in hand-specimen identification questions.

Texture: Grain Size and Its Meaning

Texture is the single most important initial observation when classifying an igneous rock. Coarse-grained rocks have crystals large enough to see with the naked eye (generally above 1 mm). Fine-grained rocks have crystals too small to see individually without a hand lens. Glassy rocks cooled so rapidly that no crystals formed at all.

Coarse grain size means slow cooling deep underground — the rock is intrusive. Fine grain size means rapid cooling, typically at the surface — the rock is extrusive. A porphyritic texture contains two populations of crystal size: large crystals called phenocrysts set in a fine-grained groundmass. Porphyritic texture tells you the magma experienced two stages of cooling: slow cooling at depth (growing phenocrysts), then rapid ascent to the surface (fine groundmass).

Key Fact

An equicrystalline texture (all crystals roughly the same size) indicates uniform cooling conditions. A porphyritic texture (phenocrysts in a finer groundmass) indicates two-stage cooling — slow at depth then rapid near the surface. These texture names appear in exam questions on igneous rocks.

Colour and Mineralogy

Igneous rocks range from very dark (ultramafic, rich in iron and magnesium) to pale (felsic, rich in silica, aluminium, sodium and potassium). The colour is a guide to mineral content. Dark minerals — olivine, pyroxene (augite), amphibole — are magnesium- and iron-rich. Pale minerals — quartz, orthoclase feldspar, plagioclase feldspar — are silica- and aluminium-rich. A rock’s colour therefore reflects its mineral make-up, and its mineral make-up reflects the chemistry of the original magma.

Peridotite — coarse-grained, very dark green to black, equicrystalline. Composed almost entirely of olivine with lesser pyroxene. No quartz, no feldspar. This is an ultramafic rock and forms the bulk of the Earth’s upper mantle. It is intrusive but comes from great depth.

Basalt — fine-grained, dark grey to black, often vesicular (containing gas bubble holes called vesicles) or porphyritic. Minerals include plagioclase feldspar, pyroxene (augite) and olivine. The most common igneous rock at the Earth’s surface; forms ocean floors and many volcanic islands. Extrusive.

Andesite — fine-grained, grey to brownish-grey, often porphyritic with visible phenocrysts of plagioclase feldspar. Named after the Andes mountains, where it is typical of subduction-zone volcanoes. More silica-rich than basalt; commonly contains hornblende as well as pyroxene. Extrusive.

Granite — coarse-grained, pale pink to white-grey, equicrystalline. Contains quartz (grey, glassy), orthoclase feldspar (pink or white), plagioclase feldspar (white), and mica (biotite = black flakes; muscovite = silver flakes). A felsic rock; forms large deep intrusive bodies called batholiths. Intrusive.

Key Fact

Summary: Peridotite (coarse, very dark, olivine + pyroxene) — Basalt (fine, dark, plagioclase + augite) — Andesite (fine, grey, plagioclase phenocrysts + pyroxene) — Granite (coarse, pale, quartz + orthoclase + mica). Only these four names are spec-listed for igneous rocks. Do not write “gabbro” or “dolerite” in your answers.

Reading a Photomicrograph

Your exam may ask you to interpret a photomicrograph — a photograph taken through a microscope of a thin slice of rock ground to 30 micrometres, allowing light to pass through. Under plane-polarised light, different minerals show different colours and extinction angles. In exam questions you are not expected to use advanced polarisation theory; instead, look for crystal shape (angular crystals = fast cooling; well-formed euhedral crystals = slow cooling), relative crystal sizes (equicrystalline vs porphyritic), and colour contrast between pale and dark minerals. These observations are enough to classify the rock into one of the four spec types.

Examiner reports consistently note that students lose marks by using rock names not on the specification. The most common offenders are gabbro (coarse dark equivalent of basalt), dolerite (medium-grained intermediate intrusive) and rhyolite (fine pale volcanic rock). None of these earn any credit. Check every answer against the four spec-listed igneous rock names: peridotite, basalt, andesite, granite. If your hand specimen is coarse-grained and dark, it is peridotite. If it is fine-grained and dark, it is basalt. If it is pale and fine-grained, check whether andesite fits rather than inventing a new name.

Similarly, avoid using “igneous rock” as your final answer in a question asking for the specific rock name. Broad categories earn partial credit at best; the exam is testing whether you can distinguish between the four types.

Classification of igneous rocks connects directly to the geological settings in which they form. The textures and mineralogy you have studied here become the foundation for the next lesson, which explores how magma viscosity and different eruptive settings produce the volcanic landforms and intrusive bodies you will encounter on geological maps.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When identifying an igneous rock from a description or photograph, always address grain size first (coarse or fine?), then colour (dark = mafic; pale = felsic), then any visible minerals. A common mistake is to identify a coarse dark rock as basalt — remember, basalt is fine-grained. Coarse and dark = peridotite. Fine and dark = basalt. Fine and grey = andesite. Coarse and pale = granite. In a “compare two features” question, you must contrast both rocks on the same property: “Basalt is fine-grained whereas granite is coarse-grained” — never describe them separately.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The four spec igneous rock types are peridotite (coarse, dark, olivine + pyroxene), basalt (fine, dark, plagioclase + augite), andesite (fine, grey, porphyritic plagioclase), and granite (coarse, pale, quartz + orthoclase + mica).
  • Texture (crystal size) reflects cooling rate: coarse = slow, intrusive; fine = fast, extrusive. Porphyritic texture = two-stage cooling, with phenocrysts forming at depth and groundmass at the surface.
  • Only use spec-listed rock names in your answers. Writing “gabbro” or “dolerite” will not earn marks.

lessons.title: Magma, Volcanoes and Igneous Bodies
lessons.description: How magma viscosity controls eruption style and how lava flows, sills, dykes and plutons are identified.
lessons.content_html:
What Controls How a Volcano Erupts?

Not all volcanoes are the same. Some gently pour out thin lava flows that travel kilometres; others explode catastrophically, hurling ash and rock high into the atmosphere. The key variable is viscosity — how easily magma flows. Viscosity is controlled mainly by silica content and temperature. High-silica magmas (like those that feed andesite and rhyolite volcanoes) are sticky and trap dissolved gases; pressure builds until the eruption is explosive. Low-silica basaltic magmas are runny, allowing gases to escape gradually, producing quiet, passive eruptions.

Eruption Styles

A fissure eruption occurs when lava erupts through a linear crack in the crust rather than from a single point. The erupted lava is typically basaltic (low viscosity) and pours out in wide, flat sheets. Iceland is the best modern example, where the Mid-Atlantic Ridge intersects the island. Fissure eruptions produce broad lava plateaux and shield volcanoes with very gentle slopes.

A central vent eruption occurs when magma reaches the surface through a single pipe or chimney. The shape of the resulting volcano depends on magma viscosity. Basaltic magma builds a shield volcano with low, gently sloping sides because the lava flows far before solidifying. Higher-viscosity magma (andesitic) builds a steeper stratovolcano with more explosive eruptions and layers of ash and lava. Explosive eruptions can produce pyroclastic material — fragments of rock and solidified lava blown into the air.

Key Fact

High silica content = high viscosity = gases cannot escape = pressure builds = explosive eruption = steep-sided volcano. Low silica content = low viscosity = gases escape gradually = passive eruption = broad, gently sloping shield volcano.

Distinctive Lava Features

Basaltic lavas that cool slowly in thick flows often develop columnar jointing. As the lava cools and contracts, it cracks into regular polygonal columns, typically six-sided, perpendicular to the cooling surface. The Giant’s Causeway in Northern Ireland is the best-known British example. The columns are a direct record of the cooling geometry of the lava.

When basaltic lava erupts underwater, the outer surface quenches immediately in the cold seawater, forming rounded blobs known as pillow lava. Each new blob of lava breaks through the hardened skin of the previous one, producing a stack of overlapping pillows. Pillow lavas in the rock record are definitive evidence of submarine volcanic activity and are abundant in ancient ocean floor sequences preserved on land.

Key Fact

Columnar jointing — hexagonal columns in basalt, formed by contraction during cooling. Example: Giant’s Causeway, Northern Ireland. Pillow lava — rounded blobs formed when lava erupts underwater and quenches rapidly. Both are diagnostic field features used to interpret ancient volcanic environments.

Intrusive Igneous Bodies

Not all magma reaches the surface. Some cools and solidifies within the crust, forming intrusions. Three types are specified: sills, dykes and plutons. Each has a characteristic shape and field relationship that you need to recognise.

A sill is injected parallel to existing rock layers — it is concordant with the bedding. A sill can be recognised in the field because it lies parallel to the rock layers above and below it, and the rocks on both sides show baking (contact metamorphism) as evidence of heat. The Great Whin Sill of northern England is a well-known example, forming the resistant crag on which Hadrian’s Wall sits.

A dyke cuts across existing rock layers — it is discordant. Dykes are typically near-vertical and can be seen in coastal cliffs as dark sheets cross-cutting paler sedimentary beds. Because the dyke post-dates the rocks it cuts, cross-cutting relationships give relative age information: the dyke is always younger than the rocks it intrudes.

A pluton is a large, irregular igneous intrusion, typically of granitic composition. Plutons form deep in the crust where magma cools very slowly, producing the coarse grain size characteristic of granite. They often dome upwards, doming the overlying rocks. When erosion strips away the surrounding material over millions of years, the resistant granite is exposed at the surface. Dartmoor and Bodmin Moor in southwest England are parts of the Cornubian batholith — a chain of exposed granite plutons.

In the field, a pluton can be recognised by its lack of internal layering (unlike a sill), its irregular contact with surrounding country rock, and the metamorphic aureole — a zone of thermally altered rock surrounding the intrusion. The larger the pluton, the wider its aureole, because more heat was available over a longer cooling period.

The specification mentions a jelly lava flow simulation, which models how viscosity affects slope angle and flow shape. In the experiment, more viscous “lava” (thicker jelly) produces a steeper, shorter flow; less viscous “lava” (runnier jelly) spreads further and produces a shallower slope angle. This directly models the difference between a shield volcano built by low-viscosity basaltic lava and a steeper stratovolcano built by more viscous andesitic material. Exam questions may ask you to interpret the model or identify its limitations — for example, jelly does not reproduce temperature gradients or real gas behaviour.

Recognising intrusive and extrusive igneous bodies in the field and on geological maps is a core skill tested throughout the course. The field relationships — whether a body is concordant or discordant, whether it has a contact metamorphic aureole, and whether surrounding rocks are baked — are the primary evidence you will use when sequencing geological events in the next section on relative dating.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on intrusive bodies often ask you to identify whether a feature is a sill or a dyke from a cross-section or map. The key rule: sills run parallel to bedding (concordant); dykes cut across bedding (discordant). For questions on volcanic eruption style, always link your answer back to silica content and viscosity — do not just state “it is more explosive” without explaining why. For the jelly experiment, state what the model shows (slope angle and flow distance as proxies for viscosity) and at least one limitation (does not model real temperature, pressure or gas escape). Slope angle comparison questions require you to state a measurement or comparative value, not just “one is steeper”.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Magma viscosity (controlled by silica content) determines eruption style: low viscosity = passive fissure or central vent eruptions building shield volcanoes; high viscosity = explosive eruptions building steeper stratovolcanoes.
  • Columnar jointing forms in thick basalt flows by contraction; pillow lava forms when basalt erupts underwater. Both are diagnostic field features for interpreting ancient volcanic environments.
  • Intrusive bodies: sills (concordant, parallel to bedding), dykes (discordant, cuts across bedding) and plutons (large, irregular, deep). Plutons are always younger than the rocks they intrude and older than any dykes or sills they feed.

lessons.title: Weathering, Erosion and Sediment Transport
lessons.description: How sediment grain size, shape and sorting record transport distance and depositional energy.
lessons.content_html:
Breaking Rocks Down: Weathering

Before sediment can travel anywhere, rock must first be broken apart. Weathering is the in-place breakdown of rock. It happens at or near the Earth’s surface where rock is exposed to the atmosphere, water and living organisms. Once weathered material is loosened from the parent rock, erosion picks it up and transport carries it away. Understanding these three linked stages — weathering, erosion, transport — is essential for interpreting the sedimentary rock record.

Physical weathering breaks rock into smaller fragments without changing its chemistry. Freeze-thaw action is the most important process in cold climates: water in a crack expands by about 9% when it freezes, exerting pressure on the crack walls until the rock fragments. Repeated freeze-thaw produces angular boulders and scree slopes directly below cliffs.

Chemical weathering involves reactions between minerals and water, oxygen or acids. Feldspar is particularly susceptible to hydrolysis — it reacts with weakly acidic rainwater to produce clay minerals and dissolved ions. Calcite dissolves readily in acidic water (carbonation), which is why limestone landscapes develop karst features such as caves and sinkholes. Iron-bearing minerals oxidise to produce the red-brown iron oxides (haematite, goethite) that colour many red sedimentary sequences.

Grain Size: The Archive of Transport Energy

Grain size is the most directly readable record of the energy conditions in the transport system. High-energy environments — fast rivers, storm beaches, strong winds — move large particles; low-energy environments — deep water, slow rivers, quiet lagoons — deposit only fine particles. Grain size classifications run from boulders and gravel (coarsest) through sand to silt and clay (finest). These categories correspond to specific environments and are used to reconstruct depositional settings from ancient rocks.

Key Fact

Coarse grain size = high-energy transport (fast river, beach, wind). Fine grain size (silt/clay) = low-energy, quiet conditions (deep sea, lake, lagoon). Grain size directly records the energy of the depositional environment and is a primary tool for palaeo-environment reconstruction.

Grain Shape: Recording Transport Distance

Fresh sediment produced by weathering is angular — the sharp corners and edges that broke from the parent rock are still intact. As grains travel, they collide with each other and with the channel bed, gradually knocking off corners and edges. The result is progressive rounding. Rounding therefore indicates transport distance: angular grains have not travelled far; well-rounded grains have been transported over long distances or have been recycled through multiple sedimentary cycles.

The environment also matters: wind transport is much more effective at rounding grains than water transport because air provides less cushioning between grains. Wind-blown (aeolian) sand grains are typically frosted and well-rounded even over shorter distances; river sand grains take longer to round because they are partly cushioned by water. Scree deposits directly below a cliff contain angular fragments — they have barely moved.

Sorting: Reading Energy Consistency

Sorting describes how uniform grain sizes are within a deposit. Well-sorted sediment has a narrow range of grain sizes; poorly sorted sediment mixes coarse and fine together. Sorting reflects the consistency of the energy in the transport system. A beach exposed to regular wave action is highly sorted because the waves repeatedly winnow out fine grains, leaving only grains of similar size. A glacial till is extremely poorly sorted because ice carries everything from clay to boulders with equal indifference and dumps it all together when the ice melts.

Key Fact

Well-sorted = consistent energy environment (e.g. aeolian dune, wave-worked beach). Poorly sorted = variable or powerful depositional event (e.g. glacial till, debris flow). Sorting is a powerful clue to environment in sedimentary rock identification questions.

Screes: Angular, poorly sorted coarse fragments. Short transport, formed directly below cliffs by freeze-thaw. No rounding has occurred.

Rivers: Mixed grain sizes in active channels; gravel and sand bars in braided rivers; finer sands and silts on floodplains. Downstream, grain size decreases and rounding increases as transport distance grows.

Shallow seas: Sand-sized grains, well-sorted by wave and tidal action. Often shows ripple marks and cross-bedding.

Deep seas: Very fine silt and clay that has settled through the water column out of suspension. Also receives turbidite deposits — graded beds of sand to mud triggered by underwater avalanches.

Wind (aeolian) dunes: Well-sorted, fine to medium sand. Frosted, well-rounded grains; large-scale cross-bedding with a characteristic dune geometry.

Porosity is the proportion of empty space in a rock. Permeability is how well fluid can move through those spaces. These two properties are easily confused in exams but they measure different things. A rock can be porous without being permeable if the pores are not connected (for example, pumice has many pores but they are isolated bubbles). Conversely, a fractured rock may be permeable despite having low porosity if the fractures form a connected network.

Well-sorted coarse sandstone tends to have both high porosity (large connected pores) and high permeability (fluid passes easily). Clay-rich shale has very small, poorly connected pores — high porosity can exist but permeability is very low because the tiny pore spaces impede fluid flow. This distinction is critical when students answer questions about groundwater aquifers or reservoir rocks for oil and gas — mixing the two terms is a documented examiner concern.

The sediment properties covered in this lesson — grain size, shape and sorting, plus porosity and permeability — directly determine which sedimentary rock types form and what environments they record. The next lesson uses this foundation to classify the spec sedimentary rocks and to show how sedimentary structures like cross-bedding and graded bedding add further detail to palaeo-environment reconstruction.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Examiner reports flag the confusion between porosity and permeability as one of the highest-frequency errors in this unit. Always define them separately: porosity = percentage of pore space; permeability = ability of fluid to flow through. Then apply them correctly: a rock can be porous but not permeable (e.g. pumice). In questions about grain size and environment, remember to link grain size to energy: state the energy level, then give the grain size it produces. For sorting questions, give an environment example: well-sorted = beach or dune; poorly sorted = glacial deposit. Never say a rock is “permeable” as evidence it would make a good aquifer — also state that the pores must be connected.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Grain size records transport energy: coarse grains = high energy; fine grains = low energy. Grain shape records transport distance: angular = short distance; rounded = long distance. Sorting records energy consistency: well-sorted = uniform energy; poorly sorted = variable or powerful events.
  • Porosity (percentage pore space) and permeability (ability of fluid to pass through) are different properties. A rock can be porous but not permeable if pore spaces are not connected.
  • Different environments leave characteristic sediment signatures: screes (angular, poorly sorted), beaches (well-sorted sand), deep sea (fine clay/silt + turbidites), aeolian dunes (well-sorted, frosted, rounded sand).

lessons.title: Sedimentary Rocks and Environments of Deposition
lessons.description: Classify breccia, conglomerate, sandstone, shale, evaporites and limestone and read the environments they record.
lessons.content_html:
Sedimentary Rocks: Reading the Past

Sedimentary rocks are an archive of Earth’s history. Every layer — its grain size, composition, fossils and sedimentary structures — carries information about the environment where it was deposited. The specification asks you to identify six main rock types and to use their properties plus sedimentary structures to interpret the environment in which they formed. This lesson covers both the classification of the rocks and the toolkit of structures you use to read them.

Clastic Sedimentary Rocks

Clastic rocks are built from fragments of older rocks. Their classification is based primarily on grain size. In order from coarsest to finest:

Breccia — coarse angular fragments (clasts larger than 2 mm, angular shape). The angularity shows short transport distance, suggesting deposition near the source — for example, in a scree at the foot of a cliff or as a fault breccia produced by crushing along a fault plane.

Conglomerate — coarse rounded fragments (clasts larger than 2 mm, rounded shape). Rounded clasts indicate long transport by a powerful agent such as a braided river or a high-energy beach. Old Red Sandstone conglomerates in Wales and Scotland are classic examples from the Devonian.

Sandstone — medium-grained (0.06–2 mm), clasts of quartz and rock fragments. Can form in rivers, beaches, dunes or shallow seas. The grain shape and sorting reveal the specific environment: well-rounded frosted grains = aeolian (desert) origin; angular to sub-rounded, poorly sorted = river origin.

Shale — very fine-grained (clay and silt particles, below 0.06 mm). Shale is the most abundant sedimentary rock, forming in low-energy quiet-water environments: deep sea, lake bottoms, tidal mudflats. It splits along thin parallel bedding planes called laminations. Black shale contains abundant organic carbon and can be a source rock for petroleum.

Key Fact

Breccia = coarse angular clasts (short transport). Conglomerate = coarse rounded clasts (long transport). Sandstone = medium grains. Shale = fine clay/silt particles, low-energy environment. Grain size decreases as transport energy decreases.

Chemical and Biochemical Sedimentary Rocks

Chemical sedimentary rocks do not form from transported fragments but from ions precipitated directly from water. Evaporites — halite (rock salt) and gypsum — form when seawater or lake water evaporates in hot, arid conditions, leaving crystals behind. The presence of an evaporite sequence in the rock record is strong evidence for a palaeo-arid environment, such as a desert sabkha or an enclosed basin cut off from the open ocean.

Limestone is mostly calcium carbonate and can form in two ways: biochemically (from the shells and skeletons of marine organisms — corals, molluscs, echinoderms) or by direct chemical precipitation from supersaturated warm seawater. Most British limestones are biochemical in origin. Carboniferous Limestone in the Pennines formed in a warm, shallow tropical sea teeming with corals and crinoids. Chalk (Cretaceous Limestone) formed from the accumulation of microscopic calcareous algae in a deeper, clearer sea.

Key Fact

Evaporites (halite, gypsum) = hot, arid, evaporating basin. Carboniferous Limestone (Pennines) = warm shallow tropical sea. Chalk = deeper, clearer Cretaceous sea. Limestone generally = marine environment with calcium carbonate source.

Sedimentary Structures

Sedimentary structures are primary features formed at the time of deposition and preserved in the rock record. They add vital information about transport direction, water depth and energy that grain size alone cannot give.

Cross-bedding forms when sand is moved by a flowing current (river or wind) and builds up as migrating dunes. The internal laminae are inclined in the direction of flow. Cross-beds in a desert sandstone are large-scale (metres high) and curved; river cross-beds are smaller-scale. The dip direction of cross-beds gives the palaeoflow direction.

Graded bedding shows coarse grains at the base of a bed fining upward to fine sand or silt at the top. It forms when a turbidite current — an underwater avalanche of sediment — flows down the continental slope. The heaviest grains settle first; fine particles drift down last. Graded beds are therefore a clear signature of deep-water turbidite environments.

Ripple marks in a rock surface indicate shallow water or a current at the time of deposition. Asymmetric ripples (one steep face, one gentle face) indicate a one-directional current; symmetric ripples indicate wave oscillation. Desiccation cracks (mud cracks) form when wet sediment exposed to air dries and shrinks — they indicate an environment that was periodically exposed, such as a tidal flat or the margin of a desert lake.

Tillite is a lithified (turned to rock) glacial till — an unsorted, unlayered mixture of clay to boulder-sized clasts. Tillites in the rock record are evidence of past glaciation. The presence of striated clasts (scratched by glacial transport) confirms a glacial origin.

Coal forms from the compaction and burial of plant material in swampy, waterlogged conditions where organic matter accumulates without full decomposition (low oxygen). Carboniferous coal seams in South Wales and Yorkshire formed in tropical delta swamps. The sequence coal — seat earth (fossil soil) — shale — limestone, repeating, is the classic Carboniferous cyclothem.

Black shale is organic-rich, formed in oxygen-poor (anoxic) deep water where organic matter cannot fully decompose. It can be a source rock for oil and gas. Desert sandstone (cross-bedded, well-rounded frosted grains, red from iron oxide) records a hot, arid continental environment.

A graphic log is a vertical column drawn to scale showing rock types and sedimentary structures from bottom (oldest) to top (youngest). Grain size is plotted on the horizontal axis — fine to the left, coarse to the right. A coarsening-upward sequence (getting coarser toward the top) indicates an increase in energy over time, such as a delta advancing into a basin. A fining-upward sequence indicates a decrease in energy, such as a river channel migrating away. Structures such as cross-beds, graded beds and ripple marks are shown as symbols within the relevant bed.

Exam questions on graphic logs ask you to identify rock types, structures, or changes in environment reading upward through the sequence. Practice naming the structures and linking them to environments: graded bed = turbidite; desiccation cracks = exposure/tidal flat; large-scale cross-beds = aeolian dune.

Together, rock type, grain properties, sedimentary structures and fossils build a complete picture of the ancient environment. The fossils found in sedimentary rocks are the focus of a later unit; for now, it is enough to know that reef corals in a limestone confirm a warm, shallow, well-oxygenated marine setting, while trace fossils (burrows) in shale indicate soft, waterlogged sea-floor sediment. This lesson completes the classification of sedimentary rocks; the next moves to metamorphic rocks and the conditions that transform existing rock without melting it.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Questions on sedimentary rocks frequently ask you to “interpret the environment of deposition” from one or more pieces of evidence. Give at least two pieces of evidence and link each explicitly to the environment. For example: “The presence of graded bedding indicates a turbidite current in a deep-marine setting; the fine grain size of the mudstone interbeds supports a deep, low-energy environment.” For graphic log questions, read upward from base to top — don’t assume the oldest is at the top. Cross-bedding dip direction questions always ask you to use the inclined laminae to determine flow direction, not the overall bed attitude. For evaporites, state both the mineral present AND the process (evaporation in hot, arid conditions).
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Six spec sedimentary rock types: breccia (coarse, angular), conglomerate (coarse, rounded), sandstone (medium), shale (fine, laminated), evaporites (halite/gypsum — arid basins), limestone (carbonate — marine).
  • Sedimentary structures provide palaeo-environment evidence: cross-bedding (current direction), graded bedding (turbidite/deep sea), ripple marks (shallow current or wave), desiccation cracks (periodic exposure).
  • Graphic logs read from base (oldest) to top (youngest); a coarsening-upward sequence indicates increasing energy; a fining-upward sequence indicates decreasing energy.

lessons.title: Metamorphic Rocks: Heat, Pressure and Texture
lessons.description: Contact and regional metamorphism, foliation, and identifying slate, schist, marble and metaquartzite.
lessons.content_html:
What Is Metamorphism?

Metamorphism is the solid-state transformation of existing rock in response to increased heat and/or pressure. The rock does not melt — if melting occurs, the process becomes igneous. Instead, minerals recrystallise into new, more stable forms, and the overall texture of the rock changes. The starting material (protolith) and the temperature and pressure conditions together determine what metamorphic rock type results. Understanding this process allows geologists to reconstruct the depth and heat conditions rocks were once subjected to, long after they have been uplifted and exposed at the surface.

A common misconception is that any heat or pressure will metamorphose a rock, or that metamorphism is “a bit of melting”. Neither is true. There is a threshold below which ordinary burial and diagenesis occur; above it, true metamorphic recrystallisation begins. The boundary is gradational rather than sharp, but for practical purposes metamorphism produces new minerals not present in the original rock.

Two Types of Metamorphism

Contact metamorphism occurs when rock is baked by heat from an igneous intrusion. The intrusion — a dyke, sill or pluton — raises temperature in the surrounding country rock. The affected zone is called the metamorphic aureole. Within the aureole, pressure is not significantly elevated, so the metamorphism is mainly thermal. The most intensely altered rock is immediately adjacent to the intrusion; alteration diminishes with distance. Clay-rich rocks near a granite pluton may be converted to hornfels — though note that hornfels itself is not on the specification as a named rock type; what you need to recognise is the concept of the aureole and the principle of thermally driven recrystallisation.

Regional metamorphism operates at a much larger scale, affecting huge areas of crust during mountain-building (orogenic) events. Both temperature and pressure increase as rocks are buried to great depth along collision zones. The Caledonian orogeny that built mountains across Scotland, Wales and Ireland subjected vast quantities of sedimentary rock to regional metamorphism — producing the slates of North Wales and the schists of the Scottish Highlands. The pressures involved are far greater than in contact metamorphism, and directed pressure (stress) is the key agent that produces the characteristic aligned textures of regional metamorphic rocks.

Key Fact

Contact metamorphism: localised around an intrusion, driven by heat alone, produces a metamorphic aureole. Regional metamorphism: large-scale, driven by both heat AND directed pressure during mountain-building, affects huge crustal volumes. The presence of directed pressure is the distinguishing factor.

Foliated and Non-Foliated Textures

The most visible effect of directed pressure in regional metamorphism is the alignment of minerals perpendicular to the stress direction. This produces a family of planar textures collectively called foliation. Foliated rocks split along these planes of aligned minerals, producing flat surfaces. The style of foliation depends on the grade (intensity) of metamorphism — how high the temperature and pressure conditions were. Not all metamorphic rocks are foliated: rocks that recrystallise under contact metamorphism, or that are composed of minerals that don’t align easily, may be non-foliated.

Slate — produced from mudstone or shale by low-grade regional metamorphism. The clay minerals recrystallise into microscopic mica grains aligned perpendicular to pressure, producing slaty cleavage. Slate splits into thin flat sheets along this cleavage. The individual mica crystals are too small to see with the naked eye — the rock looks dull and fine-grained. Classic Welsh slate (quarried at Blaenau Ffestiniog) is a textbook example.

Schist — produced from mudstone, shale or slate by medium-to-high-grade regional metamorphism. Higher temperatures cause larger mica grains to grow, visible to the naked eye as glittering flakes. The alignment of these large mica flakes produces a coarser foliation called schistosity. Schist also commonly contains index minerals such as garnet, which grow as large porphyroblasts within the foliated mica matrix. Scottish Highland schists are classic examples.

Marble — produced from limestone or chalk by metamorphism (contact or regional). Calcite grains recrystallise into a coarser interlocking mosaic. Marble is non-foliated because calcite crystals do not align easily under pressure in the way mica does. Pure marble is white; impurities in the original limestone may produce coloured or veined varieties. The rock has a granular, sugary texture when freshly broken.

Metaquartzite — produced from sandstone by metamorphism. Quartz grains recrystallise under heat and pressure into an interlocking mosaic of quartz crystals. Like marble, metaquartzite is non-foliated because quartz does not produce platy aligned crystals. It is extremely hard (hardness 7, the hardness of quartz itself), tough and resistant to weathering. The boundary between individual grains is destroyed by recrystallisation — a fresh break passes through grains, not around them (unlike sandstone where the break goes around grains).

Key Fact

Foliated: Slate (from mudstone, slaty cleavage, low grade) and Schist (from mudstone/slate, schistosity, higher grade). Non-foliated: Marble (from limestone, granular calcite) and Metaquartzite (from sandstone, interlocking quartz). Foliation requires directed pressure and platy minerals.

Marble and limestone can both be white and react with acid; the key differences are texture and crystal size. Limestone has a fine-grained or bioclastic texture (visible shell fragments or micrite); marble has a coarser, granular, interlocking crystal texture and lacks visible fossils (they were destroyed during recrystallisation). Metaquartzite and sandstone can both be made of quartz; in sandstone, breaks go around grains (the cement fails first), whereas in metaquartzite, breaks go through grains because recrystallisation has destroyed original grain boundaries.

Layered rocks are not automatically sedimentary. Schist can show pronounced foliation bands that look like sedimentary bedding. The giveaway is the alignment of mica crystals: run your finger across a schist surface and it feels rough in one direction (against the mica grain) and smooth in the other. Sedimentary layers do not show this directional mineral alignment.

Metamorphic rocks complete the three-rock-type classification of the specification. The next major topic in the course — the rock cycle — ties all three rock families together, showing how igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks are continuously transformed from one into another over geological time. Recognising the metamorphic rocks by their parent rock, metamorphic type and texture is the foundation for understanding how the rock cycle operates in continental collision and subduction settings.
lessons.exam_tip_html: Metamorphic rock identification questions often ask you to distinguish between rock types with similar appearances. Always check: is the rock foliated or non-foliated? Foliation (slaty cleavage or schistosity) confirms regional metamorphism with directed pressure. Non-foliated (marble, metaquartzite) means either contact metamorphism or a rock type without platy minerals. Remember: metamorphism does NOT involve melting — if you write that a rock “partially melted” during metamorphism you will lose marks. For questions about the metamorphic aureole, state that the aureole is caused by heat from the intrusion and that alteration decreases with distance from the contact.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Contact metamorphism is localised around intrusions and driven mainly by heat; regional metamorphism is large-scale, driven by both heat and directed pressure during mountain-building. Neither involves melting.
  • Foliated metamorphic rocks (slate, schist) form when directed pressure aligns platy minerals. Non-foliated rocks (marble, metaquartzite) form from minerals that do not align easily under pressure.
  • Parent rocks: slate and schist from mudstone/shale; marble from limestone; metaquartzite from sandstone. These four are the only spec-listed metamorphic rock types — do not use gneiss or hornfels in your answers.
